title: Paint Canvas — The PNG Is the Canvas — SnapDOM Labs
text:
⌕ Showcase Live demos Labs Video overlay New WebRTC overlay New Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range Live mirror ASCII mirror New Seamless DOM Shattered capture Showcase / Labs / Paint on a capture Labs Experiment The PNG is the canvas A paint app with no element. The board is an that SnapDOM re-exports as a PNG after every stroke. TL;DR A plugin's afterRender hook saves the rendered clone; afterClone swaps it back in on the next capture and appends the newest stroke. SnapDOM uses Canvas only for the raster export. What you're looking at Pick a color and brush size, then drag across the board. The page keeps no bitmap buffer; the drawing state lives in the plugin. Try it Draw on the board below. The line under the cursor is a local SVG path; the PNG underneath catches up about every 120ms. Brush Clear Download painting How it works A hidden source element A 420×420
off-screen holds one empty replaces the board The PNG goes into the board. The download button points at the same .src . Why this needed a plugin SnapDOM 3 can reuse eligible captures, but stateful hooks run on fresh captures and the accumulated drawing belongs to the plugin. afterClone and afterRender share one closure: afterClone adds the new mark to savedClone , afterRender saves the result for the next call, independent of capture reuse. Copy-paste example The plugin factory. Swap in your own persistence logic for any "keep building on the last capture" case: function createPaintPlugin (sourceEl) { let savedClone = null let skipNext = false let pendingStroke = null function makePath (stroke) { const path = document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'path') path.setAttribute('data-stroke-id', stroke.id) path.setAttribute('d', stroke.d) path.setAttribute('fill', 'none') path.setAttribute('stroke', stroke.color) path.setAttribute('stroke-width', stroke.size) path.setAttribute('stroke-linecap', 'round') path.setAttribute('stroke-linejoin', 'round') return path } return { name: 'paint', recordStroke (stroke) { pendingStroke = stroke }, afterClone (ctx) { if (skipNext) { skipNext = false; pendingStroke = null; return } if (savedClone) ctx.clone = savedClone.cloneNode(true) if (!pendingStroke) return const layer = ctx.clone.querySelector('.strokes') const existing = layer.querySelector(`[data-stroke-id="${pendingStroke.id}"]`) if (existing) existing.setAttribute('d', pendingStroke.d) else layer.append(makePath(pendingStroke)) }, afterRender (ctx) { savedClone = ctx.clone.cloneNode(true) pendingStroke = null }, clear () { skipNext = true } } } The usage: capture again on every stroke update, plugin included: const plugin = createPaintPlugin(canvasSource) async function render (stroke) { if (stroke) plugin.recordStroke(stroke) const img = await snapdom.toPng(canvasSource, { plugins: [plugin] }) board.replaceChildren(img) } // on clear: plugin.clear() then render() again — skipNext lets SnapDOM // clone the pristine live element once, instead of hand-building an // empty replacement clone that might miss pipeline setup. stroke recordStroke() snapdom.toPng() afterClone (restore + append) afterRender (checkpoint) Limits and things to watch Every stroke update is a full capture, so the render loop is throttled (120ms here) rather than running on every pointermove . The live path keeps the drawing instant while the PNG catches up. The skipNext flag lets clear() hand the first render after a clear to SnapDOM's own cloning pipeline; a hand-built empty clone would miss pipeline behavior added later (pseudo-elements, SVG defs inlining). title: WebGL Shatter — A Capture, Shattered — SnapDOM Labs
text: ⌕ Showcase Live demos Labs Video overlay New WebRTC overlay New Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range Live mirror ASCII mirror New Seamless DOM Shattered capture Showcase / Labs / Shattered capture Labs Experiment A capture, shattered Five WebGL shaders, one starting point: a SnapDOM capture of a live, editable card, turned into a WebGL texture. TL;DR A defineExports plugin ( shatterExport ) adds result.toShatter() , which gets a canvas through the silent ctx.exports.canvas() facade (no re-triggered beforeExport / afterExport hooks) and slices it into a grid of small canvases used as WebGL textures. Ripple, glitch, dissolve and metal need no plugin: the whole card is one texture via plain snapdom.toCanvas() . What you're looking at The card's heading and paragraph are contenteditable . SnapDOM captures the card as it renders (your text, font metrics, gradient, shadow), so the effects run on your own words. Try it Edit the card, pick an effect, press the button (it relabels per effect). Ripple and Glitch settle on their own; Dissolve ends empty and needs Reset. Metal tracks your pointer until you exit it. Shatter Ripple Glitch Dissolve Metal Live DOM Try me! This text is editable HTML. SnapDOM captures it as it renders, font, gradient and shadow included, and turns it into a WebGL texture. 100% SnapDOM Shatter Reset Edit the card's text before applying an effect: you'll see your own text, not a canned image. How it works Ripple, Glitch, Dissolve, Metal: one texture, one shader snapdom.toCanvas(card, { scale: 2 }) captures the card as one canvas, uploaded with texImage2D . A per-effect fragment shader distorts or reveals it over a fixed duration (Metal: indefinitely, tracking the pointer). The card hides while the effect plays The card's CSS visibility is set to hidden after the capture and restored when the effect finishes. Metal stays hidden until you exit it. Shatter needs more than one texture shatterExport 's defineExports(ctx) returns a shatter export. result.toShatter({ cols, rows }) first gets a canvas via ctx.exports.canvas(opts) , the core exporter called directly. That canvas is sliced into a grid The canvas is cut into cols × rows small canvases with drawImage ; each becomes its own WebGL texture at its origin cell. Physics takes over Each piece spawns with a random velocity and rotation; gravity applies every frame and pieces fade out until none are left. Why this needed a plugin SnapDOM's built-in exports ( toPng , toCanvas , toSvg , toBlob ) return one complete image. Slicing into tiles is a shatter concern, not a capture concern. defineExports is the seam for an export shape core lacks. The shatter export still needs canvas pixels, so it calls the silent ctx.exports.{img,svg,canvas,blob,png,jpeg,webp} facade, which reuses the core exporters without re-running the plugin's beforeExport / afterExport hooks: no recursion, no duplicate firing. The other four effects use no plugin; most creative uses of a capture need none. defineExports is for a new output shape ; reach for toCanvas() first. Copy-paste example The plugin factory. cols / rows set the grid: function shatterExport (options = {}) { const { cols: defaultCols = 14, rows: defaultRows = 9 } = options return { name: 'shatter', defineExports (ctx) { return { shatter: async (_ctx2, opts = {}) => { const cols = opts.cols || defaultCols const rows = opts.rows || defaultRows // Reuse the core canvas exporter directly — this does NOT // re-run beforeExport/afterExport, so it's safe to call from // inside another export. const canvas = await ctx.exports.canvas(opts) const pw = canvas.width / cols const ph = canvas.height / rows const pieces = [] for (let ry = 0; ry Usage. The plugin is local to this capture; toShatter() appears on the result beside toPng / toCanvas : const result = await snapdom(card, { plugins: [shatterExport({ cols: 16, rows: 11 })] }) const { pieces } = await result.toShatter() // pieces[i] = { u, v, du, dv, canvas } — grid position (0..1) plus a // small <canvas>, ready to hand to texImage2D as its own WebGL texture The other four effects skip the plugin: one capture, one texture: const canvas = await snapdom.toCanvas(card, { scale: 2 }) const tex = makeTexture(canvas) // gl.texImage2D(..., canvas) card snapdom(plugins) result.toShatter() ctx.exports.canvas() slice into pieces WebGL textures Limits and things to watch The ctx.exports.canvas() facade is documented in PLUGIN_SPEC.md . A 16×11 grid makes 176 pieces; finer grids add draw calls, textures and memory. title: ASCII Mirror — a live element as text — SnapDOM Labs
text: ⌕ Showcase Live demos Labs Video overlay New WebRTC overlay New Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range Live mirror ASCII mirror New Seamless DOM Shattered capture Showcase / Labs / ASCII mirror Labs Experiment A live element, as text A card with text and a spinning CSS cube. The right side is the same element redrawn as ASCII art on every frame, through the stream plugin. TL;DR One call: asciiStream(el, { onText }) . Under it, stream() keeps a canvas in step with the card, and asciiFromCanvas() , the function behind the ascii-export plugin, turns each frame into characters. No capture result in between: the canvas goes straight from one to the other. What you're looking at The left card is editable HTML on a white background with solid-colored boxes, the shape the stream plugin patches best. The right pane is a <pre> . On every frame the plugin hands over its canvas, the text is recomputed and replaced. Pick a character set, change the width, or switch to color to see each character carry the pixel it came from. Try it Charset Classic Blocks Dots Binary Width 90 Color Invert Editable DOM contenteditable + CSS 3D Hello, text Keystrokes and the spinning cube become patched frames, then characters. S N A P D O ASCII output asciiStream() starting… Loading the stream plugin… How it works stream() watches the card The first frame is a full SnapDOM capture. After that, a keystroke is traced to the nearest box with a solid background and only that subtree is captured and drawn into its rectangle. The cube is different: a 3D transform leaves the flow, so while it spins every frame is a full capture, capped here at 15 fps. Stop the cube (pause it from devtools, or delete it) and the stats switch to patches. asciiFromCanvas() does the pixel work On each repaint it downsamples the canvas to one pixel per character, maps luminance to the charset and returns a string, or colored HTML when format: 'html' . It is the same code the toAscii() export uses, exported on its own so it runs on any drawable: a stream frame, a video, your own canvas. asciiStream() is the two together It takes the ascii options and the stream options in one object and calls onText(text, frame) after every repaint. The handle it returns is the stream's: ready , stats , stop() . The <pre> is replaced textContent for plain text, innerHTML for the colored version. Nothing else on the page is touched. Copy-paste example import { asciiStream } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/ascii-export' const out = document.querySelector('pre') const live = asciiStream(document.querySelector('#card'), { width: 90, fps: 15, onText: text => { out.textContent = text } }) await live.ready // later: live.stop() Without the sugar it is two calls: stream(el, { onFrame: f => out.textContent = asciiFromCanvas(f.canvas, { width: 90 }) }) . The same shape works for any pixel-level step on a frame, or for a video element instead of a stream. Limits and things to watch Patches need a solid background somewhere above the change; on a gradient card every frame is a full capture. Width above 140 columns makes the conversion visible in the frame budget on slow machines. Color mode produces one <span> per character, so keep it under 100 columns. title: Stop Motion — You Choose the Frames — SnapDOM Labs
text: ⌕ Showcase Live demos Labs Video overlay New WebRTC overlay New Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range Live mirror ASCII mirror New Seamless DOM Shattered capture Showcase / Labs / Stop motion Labs Experiment You choose the frames Pose an actor, press the shutter, move on. The sequence is the poses you kept, like a physical stop-motion rig. TL;DR A small plugin's afterRender hook fires once per capture and hands back ctx.dataURL . The plugin collects those URLs into an ordered array; the player sets the rhythm. What you're looking at Three sliders pose an actor on a small stage. Capture pose captures the stage and appends it to a filmstrip. Play flips through the filmstrip at a fixed interval. Try it Pose the actor, capture a few poses, then press Play. Each thumbnail is a separate SVG snapshot. Horizontal Vertical Rotation + Capture pose Play Capture at least two poses. How it works The plugin factory closes over a counter frameCollector(onFrame) returns a plugin with one private index : the frame count, no clone or DOM reference. Moving a slider captures nothing The sliders update inline styles and a CSS custom property on the live #actor . SnapDOM is not involved yet. Capture pose runs one capture The button calls snapdom(poseScene, { plugins: [collector] }) against the live stage, in whatever pose the sliders show. afterRender fires with the finished context Once SnapDOM renders the SVG, afterRender(ctx) increments the counter and calls back with { index, url: ctx.dataURL } . The page pushes the URL into an array capturedFrames.push(frame.url) , plus a thumbnail in the filmstrip. The plugin knows nothing about the filmstrip. Play iterates the array on a timer Play walks capturedFrames for a few loops, swapping .src on an interval. The plugin is not involved. Why this needed a plugin In the paint-canvas and target-range labs a plugin mutates ctx.clone and persists it, so each capture builds on the last. Here ctx.clone is left alone and each pose is a self-contained render. The afterRender hook centralizes frame collection via ctx.dataURL . An application could instead read result.url after awaiting snapdom() ; the callback keeps the bookkeeping in one place. Copy-paste example The plugin factory. It collects dataURLs and nothing else: function frameCollector (onFrame) { let index = 0 return { name: 'frame-collector', afterRender (ctx) { index += 1 onFrame({ index, url: ctx.dataURL }) }, reset () { index = 0 } } } The usage: capture a pose, read the frame back through the callback: const capturedFrames = [] const collector = frameCollector(frame => { capturedFrames.push(frame.url) }) // runs once per "Capture pose" click, against whatever // pose the sliders are showing at that moment await snapdom(poseScene, { plugins: [collector] }) slider input live style change (no capture) Capture pose snapdom() afterRender (ctx.dataURL) capturedFrames.push() Limits and things to watch The collector's afterRender hook is stateful, so in v3 each pose runs a fresh capture; resource caches can still be reused. Each SVG data URL stays in memory, so the filmstrip grows with frame count and content. title: Seamless DOM WebGL: text that isn't text — SnapDOM Labs
text: ⌕ Showcase Live demos Labs Video overlay New WebRTC overlay New Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range Live mirror ASCII mirror New Seamless DOM Shattered capture Showcase / Labs / Seamless DOM Labs Experiment The text you see isn't text Click into the box below and type. Every glyph is a WebGL texture rendered from the last SnapDOM capture. The editable DOM is invisible, and updates cross-fade in. TL;DR A transparent contenteditable proxy gives the browser a real caret and keystrokes; a hidden source element mirrors the text and is what SnapDOM captures. A defineExports plugin feeds each capture into a WebGL renderer that double-buffers two textures and cross-fades between them. What you're looking at You get a blinking caret and text selection. The glyphs are pixels in a WebGL texture captured from a hidden DOM element and mixed into the canvas under your cursor. The shader dropdown changes only what the fragment shader does with the finished frame. Try it Type, paste, or press Enter. The caret and selection are real; the letters are not. Shader Faithful Hologram CRT Liquid Kaleidoscope Melt Datamosh Neon Edge Live DOM signal Type here This text is real DOM, but you're seeing it as a WebGL texture kept in sync by SnapDOM. LIVE GPU Hidden DOM double-buffered texture starting… How it works A transparent proxy owns the caret The .input-layer sits on top of the WebGL canvas with transparent text and background. It gives the browser somewhere to place a caret and receives keyboard and paste events; the caret and selection stay visible. Every edit is mirrored to a hidden element On every input event, paste, and Enter (a beforeinput override inserts a literal newline instead of letting contenteditable create a new <div> ), the proxy's text is copied into the hidden #dom-source element and refresh() runs. refresh() coalesces bursts Same dirty / working loop as the live-mirror demo: input during a capture is flagged dirty and picked up by the running loop. It captures #dom-source with the seamlessWebgl plugin. The plugin exports into the renderer The plugin's defineExports returns a webgl export that hands the capture's URL to renderer.update(ctx.export.url) instead of returning an image. The idle texture is loaded, not the visible one SeamlessRenderer.update() loads the new capture into whichever of its two textures ( current or next ) is off screen, then starts a roughly 110ms blend toward it. The shader mixes, then the effect applies The fragment shader mixes beforeImage and afterImage by a blend uniform that ramps 0 1 over that window; the selected shader runs on the result. Why this needed a plugin SnapDOM's core exports return a finished image. defineExports lets a plugin register a named export (here webgl ) that does something else with the render, such as pushing it into one of two alternating GPU textures. The difference from the live-mirror demo is architectural. Splitting the caret owner from the capture source makes the transition seamless: the canvas never waits on a capture, it is always mid-blend between two textures it already has while the hidden source is captured again. Copy-paste example The plugin factory forwards a capture's URL to the renderer you hand it: function seamlessWebgl (renderer) { let started = 0 let elapsed = 0 return { name: 'seamless-webgl', beforeSnap () { started = performance.now() }, afterRender () { elapsed = performance.now() - started }, defineExports () { return { webgl: async ctx => { const canvas = await renderer.update(ctx.export.url) perfLabel.textContent = `${elapsed.toFixed(0)} ms · texture swapped` return canvas } } } } } The usage calls the export through the generic capture.to('webgl') rather than capture.toWebgl() . Both work; .to(name) invokes a plugin-defined export without SnapDOM knowing its name ahead of time: const plugin = seamlessWebgl(renderer) let dirty = false let working = false async function refresh () { dirty = true if (working) return working = true while (dirty) { dirty = false const capture = await snapdom(source, { plugins: [plugin] }) await capture.to('webgl') } working = false } input sync #dom-source refresh() capture.to('webgl') renderer.update() blend 0 1 shader Limits and things to watch The transparent-proxy trick works for plain text only; rich text and IME composition edge cases need more care. This proxy reduces Enter to a literal newline and paste to plain text. Double-buffering costs one extra WebGL texture of GPU memory over the live-mirror demo, worth it only when the crossfade is the point. title: Target Range — Every Shot Hits the Clone — SnapDOM Labs
text:
⌕ Showcase Live demos Labs Video overlay New WebRTC overlay New Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range Live mirror ASCII mirror New Seamless DOM Shattered capture Showcase / Labs / Target range Labs Experiment Every shot hits the clone A shooting gallery where the board is a PNG. Each shot re-captures on top of the shots before it; the live target in the DOM stays clean. TL;DR A plugin's afterRender hook saves the rendered clone; afterClone swaps it back in on the next capture with a new bullet hole appended. The accumulation lives in the plugin's closure. What you're looking at Ten shots, a swaying crosshair, a ring-scored target. The board is one , replaced after every shot with a new snapdom.toPng() result. Try it Aim, click to fire. The reticle drifts and kicks after every shot, and the drift grows as ammo runs out. The marker that appears is the exported PNG. 0 Score 10 Shots 0 Best Ready? 10 shots. The reticle sways and kicks with every shot, so compensate for the drift. Start Restart Download target The download button uses the returned by the last snapdom.toPng() call; no second capture. How it works A hidden source element A 340×340
off-screen holds one SVG target built from a ring definition. SnapDOM captures this element, not the visible board. The shot is scored locally On click, the reticle's position after sway and recoil (not the raw mouse position) is converted to a percentage and scored against the ring radii. The resulting { xPct, yPct, color } goes to plugin.addHit() . addHit() appends a marker to the saved clone On the first shot the plugin clones the live source once. Each call appends a jagged, randomized torn-paper hole, positioned in percentage coordinates so it survives the render round trip. snapdom.toPng() runs again, plugin included The demo calls snapdom.toPng(target, { plugins: [plugin] }) again, same as the first shot. afterClone swaps in the saved clone The plugin replaces ctx.clone with the clone it has been building, holes included, instead of the hole-free source. afterRender checkpoints the result The plugin clones the rendered result as the baseline for the next shot. The output replaces the board The PNG goes into the board. Why this needed a plugin SnapDOM 3 can reuse eligible captures, but stateful hooks run on fresh captures and the accumulated holes belong to the plugin. afterClone and afterRender share one closure with addHit() : it adds the mark to savedClone , afterClone swaps that clone in, afterRender saves the result for the next call, independent of capture reuse. Copy-paste example The plugin factory, usable for any "keep building on the last capture" case: function createHitboardPlugin (sourceEl) { let savedClone = null return { name: 'hitboard', afterClone (ctx) { if (savedClone) ctx.clone = savedClone.cloneNode(true) }, afterRender (ctx) { savedClone = ctx.clone.cloneNode(true) }, addHit (xPct, yPct, color) { if (!savedClone) savedClone = sourceEl.cloneNode(true) if (getComputedStyle(savedClone).position === 'static') { savedClone.style.position = 'relative' } const hit = document.createElement('div') hit.style.cssText = ` position: absolute; left: ${xPct}%; top: ${yPct}%; width: 24px; height: 24px; margin: -12px 0 0 -12px; pointer-events: none; ` hit.innerHTML = bulletHoleMarkup(color) savedClone.appendChild(hit) }, reset () { savedClone = null } } } The usage: score the shot, tell the plugin, capture again: const plugin = createHitboardPlugin(target) function shoot (xPct, yPct) { const { color } = scoreAt(xPct, yPct) plugin.addHit(xPct, yPct, color) return snapdom.toPng(target, { plugins: [plugin] }) } // on restart: plugin = createHitboardPlugin(target) — a fresh closure, // not plugin.reset(), so a stale reference from the finished game can't // leak a hole into the new one. shot addHit() snapdom.toPng() afterClone (restore + append) afterRender (checkpoint) Limits and things to watch addHit() initializes savedClone from the live source on first call, so the plugin needs no priming. reset() sets it back to null and the next capture re-clones the pristine source. Simpler than Paint Canvas 's skipNext flag: a restart is a hard reset, not a stroke boundary to detect mid-stream. title: Live Video Overlays from Plain HTML — SnapDOM Labs
text: ⌕ Showcase Live demos Labs Video overlay New WebRTC overlay New Stop motion Paint on a capture Capture stages Target range Live mirror ASCII mirror New Seamless DOM Shattered capture Showcase / Labs / Video overlay Labs Experiment Live video overlays from plain HTML A scoreboard, a lower third, a stream chat: HTML and CSS composited over live video in the browser, in Chrome, Firefox and Safari. No OBS, no server. TL;DR The stream plugin keeps the overlay as a canvas that repaints only the boxes that changed; streamTexture uploads those rectangles to WebGL, where a shader composites them over the video and gives the look: clean, shine, CRT, hologram, glitch, or liquid glass refracting the footage under each panel. The output is a canvas. No browser flag. Try it Sports TV runs a broadcast package over a simulated match; press Goal or wait for one. Streamer uses your camera; Share screen puts your game behind the overlay, you in a circle. Change the look, drag the pieces, record a clip, or press Edit for the HTML and CSS. Sports TV Streamer Clean Liquid glass Shine CRT Hologram Glitch Goal! Camera Share screen Record Edit starting Liquid Refraction Bevel Frost Dispersion HTML CSS The overlay is this HTML and CSS. Panels with class glass paint var(--panel) , which the Liquid glass look turns into refracting glass shaped by the box and its border-radius ; give them position: absolute to drag them. data-clock shows a clock, data-rotate="one|two" cycles its text. The stage below is 960 by 540 pixels. How it works The HTML is a real DOM element Your markup goes into a 960 by 540 stage on this page, with your CSS nested under it. stream() turns it into a canvas that repaints only what changed The first frame is a full SnapDOM capture. After that, a change is traced to the nearest box that can repaint on its own, and only that subtree is captured. A patched frame matches a full capture pixel for pixel. streamTexture() uploads the dirty rectangles On WebGL2 only the changed rectangles reach the GPU, usually a few percent of the texture per frame. The shader composites the video and the overlay Most looks read only the overlay texture: a light sweep, scanlines and glow, a hologram tint, glitch slices on a goal. Liquid glass also reads the layout: each frame, every .glass panel's box and border-radius become a rounded-rectangle distance field, joined by a smooth minimum with the drop under the pointer, so nearby shapes melt together. A spring makes each shape trail its box, so moving pieces stretch and wobble. Inside, the footage is sampled through a lens: pulled inward at the rim, frosted, colour-split, darkened over bright backgrounds so white text stays legible. The streamed HTML goes on top. The program output is a canvas It records to MP4 or WebM with recordCanvas() , or goes out as a WebRTC track with captureStream() , overlay included. The code The SnapDOM part is short. The rest is a full-screen fragment shader. import { stream, streamTexture } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/stream' const gl = canvas.getContext('webgl2') const overlay = streamTexture(gl) stream(stage, { embedFonts: false, onFrame: (frame) => overlay.update(frame), // uploads frame.rects only }) // every animation frame: upload the video, pass each .glass box to the shader, draw for (const el of stage.querySelectorAll('.glass')) { const r = el.getBoundingClientRect() // relative to the stage rects.push(r.left - base.left, r.top - base.top, r.width, r.height) } Limits The glass shape is the box and its border-radius , one radius per box; other shapes need their own distance function in the shader. The texture is pixels: links and buttons in it are not clickable. A box over a translucent background ( rgba() with alpha below 1) cannot repaint alone and forces a full repaint. Keep glass boxes free of background colour. Footage from another origin needs CORS. Previous Live demos Next WebRTC overlay

title: SnapDOM PDF — open-source pdf export
text: Export plugins PDF Vector All plugins PDF reference Full API reference Source · MIT All plugin demos Live PDF export Live sample Report A4 ledger Multilingual text Form controls Transparent artwork Page size Fit to content A4 Letter Selectable text Fillable fields Generate PDF Editable source Generated output Nothing generated yet. Previous Next Edit the source, then generate a PDF. Code for this demo Build / Plugins / PDF Official plugin · MIT Export a searchable PDF. Capture a live element, add selectable text and links, and paginate it into a PDF in your browser. Open source PDF is MIT-licensed source inside packages/plugins/pdf . Available in @zumer/snapdom-plugins@4 for SnapDOM 3.x. These demos use the official plugin; npm run site uses your local build. How it works The page image plus a PDF text layer The page image is SnapDOM's capture. The plugin places a second, invisible text layer over it using positions derived from SnapDOM's final serialized clone. No headless browser or separate layout engine rebuilds the page. Fidelity The visible result preserves SnapDOM's rendering of gradients, shadows, filters, web fonts and the rest of the captured element. The text layer adds document behaviour without replacing that image. Multilingual text CJK, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic, Hebrew and emoji carry a /ToUnicode CMap, so selection, search and copy work for every script, whether or not a glyph travels with the file. Pagination Ten page sizes from A6 to tabloid, a custom [width, height] in points, or one page the size of the element. Breaks are pulled up off table rows, list items and figures, and break-before: page is honoured. Headers, footers and page numbers take their room out of the page rather than covering it. Text-form headers/footers and page numbers are real PDF text; Element-form bands are captured images. What reaches the layer Text nodes, input / textarea / select values, open shadow roots, and CSS transforms: rotation and skew go into the text matrix. Passwords are bulleted, never written. What does not Layout-hidden and transparent content is removed. Ambiguous clip, mask and filter geometry is omitted fail-safe. Arbitrary overlap is different: a rectangle or blur can cover pixels without removing the underlying semantic text, so it is not a redaction mechanism. Embedded fonts The faces the page painted with travel inside the file, subset to the glyphs the document actually drew. A ~320 kB face reaches a Latin page as a few kB. Turn on vectorText and eligible runs are painted as real vector glyphs instead of sitting invisible over the raster: crisp at any zoom, and an image-free export of the same page drops from ~420 kB to ~22 kB. Fillable forms A captured form is still a form. Inputs, textareas, checkboxes, radio groups and selects become real AcroForm fields (fillable, tabbable, extractable) carrying their name, value, options, checked state, required and read-only flags, and the accessible label as the tooltip a screen reader speaks. No JavaScript actions, no submit URLs, and a password field is written empty. Encrypted downloads A file that leaves the browser can be AES-256 encrypted on the way out, so the download itself is protected once it is attached and forwarded. Standard security handler revision 6, from the browser's own crypto.subtle , so no cipher code ships in the plugin and RC4 is not offered at any setting. A user password is required: the flavour of "encryption" that opens without asking is refused rather than produced. Identity and determinism Title, author, subject and keywords reach /Info and a mirrored XMP packet; a title also makes viewers show the document's name instead of its filename. Dates are never invented and the trailer /ID is a content hash, so the same unencrypted input produces the same bytes. Progress, cancellation, diagnostics Long exports report progress and take an AbortSignal . Every fidelity trade-off is also a structured diagnostic with a stable code, so a build can gate on "no annotations lost" without parsing console prose. Transparency A capture with alpha carries a Flate /SMask . Flatten it onto a colour to remove the mask. For every image, codec: auto compares JPEG with lossless Flate and keeps the smaller result. The lossless candidate is written in the narrowest colour space that reproduces the pixels exactly, which is one byte per pixel instead of three on the grey or few-coloured regions most page artwork turns out to be. Document features Headings become bookmarks and named destinations. Optional generated contents, repeated table headers, cover/back pages and watermarks make this a document exporter rather than a canvas wrapper. Accessibility structure Tagged output covers headings, prose, lists, tables, sections and figures. The PDF/UA-1 claim is earned, never configured : it is written only when every text operation rode an embedded face, the export is tagged, has a language and displays a title, and no painted image lacks alternative text. When a blocker remains the claim is withheld and the blocker is named . Ships as A minified ES module to ship, an unminified one to read, TypeScript declarations, versioned reference and MIT license. Browser use without a bundler requires an import map for the external SnapDOM peer. Verified by The full Chromium suite parses PDFs back with pdf.js, checks raw bytes (xref offsets, stream lengths, the lot), and one fixture compares the text layer against pixels . A separate gate imports and executes both plugin builds in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. That is a three-engine API/artifact smoke, not three full layout suites. Quick start Add PDF export to SnapDOM Register the plugin once and every capture gains toPdf() alongside toPng() and toCanvas() . It reuses the existing capture rather than running a second capture engine. import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import pdf from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/pdf' snapdom.plugins(pdf()) const shot = await snapdom(document.querySelector( '#report' ), { scale: 2 , dpr: 1 }) const blob = await shot.toPdf({ page: 'a4' , // 'fit' | 'a4' | 'a5' | 'letter' | … margin: 36 , // points header: { left: 'ACME' , right: 'Q3 ledger' }, // real text, or pass an element pageNumbers: true , // or { format, align, size, color } codec: 'auto' , // smaller JPEG or lossless Flate tagged: true , // structure, not a PDF/UA badge download: 'report.pdf' // also downloads it }) On first PDF export, the plugin reads SnapDOM's final serialized clone, not the original live DOM, so real node removal/replacement stays aligned. Page regions are rasterized lazily and cached for later exports. Geometry-preserving final-artifact replacements stay aligned; aspect-preserving width/height scaling is allowed, while incompatible viewBox, root paint/layout or intrinsic-aspect changes fail instead of guessing coordinates. For secrets, remove or replace the node/text; never treat an overlay or blur as redaction. Capture-model options ( formValues , shadow , breakAvoid , outline ) belong in pdf({ ... }) . page 'fit' · one page the size of the element, or a3 / a4 / a5 / a6 / b4 / b5 / letter / legal / tabloid / executive , or [width, height] in points. orientation 'portrait' or 'landscape' . margin Points. 24 . codec auto keeps the smaller JPEG or lossless Flate image. quality Quality of the JPEG candidate. 0.92 . It changes nothing while the lossless candidate wins, which on page artwork is until roughly 0.5 . deflate Deflate the content streams. true . text Emit the selectable layer. true . Turn it off and you get an image-only PDF. links Emit same-document destinations and safe http: , https: , mailto: and tel: annotations. true . image Draw the page image. true . Set false for an image-free PDF that keeps the enabled text, links and structure. Element headers, footers and watermarks are then omitted; cover/back pages keep semantics without their raster. formValues Put input / textarea / select values in the layer. true . shadow Walk open shadow roots. true . breakAvoid Keep page breaks off rows, list items and figures. true . outline Bookmarks from headings; capture-time. true . forms Measure form controls so the export can write fillable fields; capture-time. true . tagged / lang Structure the document and set its spoken language. embedFonts Embed the capture's @font-face binaries, subset to the glyphs the document drew. true . 'full' embeds unsubsetted; false embeds nothing. vectorText Paint eligible runs as real vector glyphs instead of leaving them invisible over the raster. false . RTL and complex scripts stay on the raster. fields Write measured controls as real AcroForm fields. true . false keeps their values in the invisible layer instead. repeatHeaders Repeat a continuing table's thead pixels and text. header A running head across the top of every page. Give it a string or three independent segments, { left, center, right } , each of which can be a function of the page number. Either way it is drawn as real text : selectable, searchable, crisp at any zoom. Pass an element instead and it is captured, for when you need a logo. Either way it takes its height out of the printable area rather than sitting over it. footer The same, along the bottom. pageNumbers true , or { format, align, size, color, font } . Drawn as real PDF text rather than captured, so it stays crisp at any zoom and is searchable like the rest. It sits in the bottom margin, under a footer if there is one. debugText Paint the invisible layer in red, so you can see where it sits. false . cover / toc / back Captured front/back pages and generated linked contents. watermark Text or an element, drawn over every page. encrypt {userPassword, ownerPassword, permissions} . AES-256 (R6). The password is what protects the file; the permission flags are a request a viewer may honour. Needs https or localhost. meta {title, author, subject, keywords, creator, created, modified} /Info and XMP. Dates are written only when you pass them. onProgress ({phase, done, total}) per step, for exports long enough to need a bar. signal An AbortSignal . Aborting rejects between pages with AbortError and produces nothing. onReport The structured diagnostics report once the Blob is finished, with stable warning codes, counts, pages, bytes, fields and annotations. download A filename. Downloads the blob as well as returning it. backgroundColor Flatten at capture, plugin-default or export time. Resolution remains a snapdom(...) concern. Read the complete option, warning and limits reference Open source Included in the SnapDOM monorepo The PDF plugin is available as MIT-licensed source in packages/plugins/pdf . PDF and Vector are available on npm in @zumer/snapdom-plugins 4.x and require SnapDOM 3.x. Read the reference · SnapDOM on GitHub Before you ask Questions Can I use it in something I sell to a client? Yes. The MIT license permits commercial use, modification and redistribution. Keep the license notice with redistributed copies. Is the text really selectable, or is it OCR? It is selectable without OCR. Eligible text is placed from browser geometry in SnapDOM's final serialized clone, so structural exclusions and geometry-preserving replacements stay aligned with the capture. Ambiguous paint effects are omitted fail-safe. Download a sample and copy a paragraph. Is it open source? Yes. The PDF plugin is part of the SnapDOM monorepo under the MIT license. Can I read the code? Yes. Its source, reference and browser test suites live in packages/plugins/pdf in the SnapDOM monorepo. Does it need a server? The exporter itself runs in the browser and returns a Blob ; it does not upload the PDF. SnapDOM may still fetch resources used by the page, or use a proxy if your application configured one. Why is the text raster and not vector? By default the visible pixels preserve SnapDOM's own rendering instead of asking a PDF layout engine to reinterpret the page. Zoom far past the selected capture resolution and you will see pixels. The invisible layer adds selection, search and copy without repainting the type. You can have the other model: vectorText: true paints eligible runs as real glyphs from the embedded fonts, and with image: false the result is a small, fully vector text PDF. It is opt-in because it is a different fidelity promise. RTL and complex scripts are never painted this way, and they stay on the raster. Can the PDF be password protected? Yes. encrypt: { userPassword } writes an AES-256 file, so the download is protected once it is shared. It uses the browser's own crypto, so no cipher code ships in the plugin, and it needs a secure context: https or localhost. Two things it will not do. It does not offer RC4 or the older PDF revisions, whose 40-bit key is broken. And it will not write an empty user password: that produces a file that is encrypted and still opens without asking anyone anything, which is worse than no protection because it looks like some. Permission flags (no printing, no copying) are written when you ask for them, but they are a request a viewer may honour, not a lock. Which browsers? The complete fixture suite is Chromium-only. Both plugin builds must also pass the release artifact smoke in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. That supports the plugin/API contract in all three; it does not pretend every complex layout has the same three-engine coverage.

A global/IIFE SnapDOM script cannot satisfy the plugin's ESM peer import. Requires @zumer/snapdom >=3.0.0 <4 . SnapDOM 3 is the floor. The exporter reads v3's immutable capture metadata, requested export options and pre-decode canvas crops, which 2.x does not expose. The fixture suite runs against the published 3.0.0. Registering The module exports the same pdf factory as default and named export. It does not export a standalone toPdf(element) helper. import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import pdf, { pdf as namedPdf } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/pdf' snapdom.plugins(pdf()) // every later capture const local = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [pdf()] }) // this capture const shot = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#report'), { scale: 2, dpr: 1 }) const blob = await shot.toPdf({ page: 'a4' }) const same = await shot.to('pdf', { page: 'a4' }) Both exports return Promise with type application/pdf . TypeScript declarations add toPdf(options?: PdfExportOptions) to SnapDOM's CaptureResult . Two option moments The PDF model is derived lazily from SnapDOM's final serialized clone on first export, not from the original live DOM. Five options control that model and must be fixed on pdf() before capture: Option Default Meaning formValues true Include visible values of text controls and the selected option. Passwords become bullets. shadow true Walk open shadow roots as the flattened tree. breakAvoid true Measure atomic blocks for pagination. outline true Headings become bookmarks. Use a selector string or false . forms true Measure form controls (kind, name, value, options, geometry, painted style) so the export can write fillable fields. false skips the measurement. Every export option may also be a factory default. A value in toPdf() wins. A capture-time option passed there warns and is ignored. A custom outline selector is evaluated against the final flattened artifact, including matching open-shadow and slotted headings. Page and pagination Option Default Meaning page 'fit' fit ; A3–A6; B4/B5; letter, legal, tabloid, executive; or [width,height] in points. orientation 'portrait' portrait or landscape ; irrelevant to fit . margin 24 Points on all sides; irrelevant to fit . repeatHeaders true Repeat a continuing table's pixels and selectable text. Breaks are pulled off table rows, list items, definitions, figures, blockquotes, replaced content, short leaf blocks and break-inside:avoid content. Declared page breaks are honoured unless they only create an empty page. A block taller than a page still has to split. Only repeats. Its repeated copy has no repeated link annotations, and a header taller than half a page is refused with a warning. Raster Option Default Meaning image true Draw the visible SnapDOM raster. false makes an image-free PDF; Element headers, footers and watermarks are omitted. codec 'auto' Compare JPEG and lossless Flate per image and keep the smaller; or pin jpeg / flate . quality capture / .92 Quality of the JPEG candidate only, taken from the capture when the export does not set one. It reaches nothing when Flate wins, and on ordinary page artwork Flate wins until roughly 0.5 : on a 35-page report 0.92 , 0.8 and 0.6 all produce a byte-identical 11.3 MB, 0.4 gives 10.8 MB and 0.2 gives 10.1 MB. An export whose lowered quality changed nothing says so in the console. scale / dpr on the capture Neither moves a point of geometry, because a PDF has no device to match, so the page box and the text layer are identical whatever they are. They multiply the page image's pixels, and they multiply together : on a 35-page report scale:1, dpr:2 and scale:2, dpr:1 both give 11.3 MB, against 5.1 MB at 1×1 and 24.4 MB at 2×2. dpr defaults to the exporting machine's devicePixelRatio , so pin it if you want the same bytes from a laptop and from CI. backgroundColor capture / null Flatten this PDF export onto a colour instead of carrying alpha. Capture resolution belongs to snapdom(el,{ scale, dpr, width, height }) . Page regions are rasterized lazily and cached on the capture for later exports. A codec, quality or flattening change may still require a new encode; codec:'auto' compares two candidates. When CompressionStream is unavailable, auto uses JPEG and a pinned Flate request warns before falling back. A transparent raster uses a soft mask; flattening usually makes the file smaller. The colour space is earned, not configured Before a region is compressed it is inspected once, and the Flate candidate is written in the narrowest PDF colour space that reproduces those pixels exactly : /DeviceGray when every pixel has r == g == b , an /Indexed palette when the region drew 256 colours or fewer, and /DeviceRGB otherwise. The first two are one byte per pixel instead of three. Page artwork is overwhelmingly one of the first two. Across this project's fixtures, 22 of 29 page regions are grey in every pixel and 23 of 29 fit in a palette, so the effect on real documents is large: a 30-page report drops from 12.4 MB to 8.7 MB, a page of prose by 37%, a typography page by 43%. Regions that genuinely need /DeviceRGB are unchanged, and nothing is approximated to earn the narrowing: the stream inflates back to the original pixels, which the fixture suite asserts by decoding it and comparing pixel for pixel. The narrowing also widens the gap Flate already had over DCT. On every fixture in this project Flate now wins by between 1.7× and 3.6×, which is why quality so often reaches nothing. It is not made to win everywhere. A photographic region is neither grey nor 256 colours, so it narrows to nothing and JPEG can still be the smaller answer. That is exactly why auto still runs the comparison. Text and links Option Default Meaning text true Emit invisible selectable/searchable text. links true Emit external URI and in-document annotations. debugText false Paint the layer red and leave content streams readable. Runs are measured from SnapDOM's final serialized clone, one word at a time. Visible form values, open shadow roots, text transforms and logical bidi text are included. Real removals/replacements from exclude , filter , resolveNode , afterClone , clip , or a geometry-preserving afterRender replacement of the final serialized tree/URL stay aligned. A replacement that changes viewBox, root paint/layout attributes or intrinsic aspect/geometry incompatibly fails instead of producing a misaligned layer. Uniform width/height scaling that preserves aspect is allowed. Layout-hidden and transparent text is excluded. Same-document fragments become PDF destinations. External annotations accept only http: , https: , mailto: and tel: . Missing fragment targets, malformed URLs and other schemes produce no annotation and a warning. Visual occlusion is not redaction. Remove or replace confidential nodes/text. Do not rely on an overlay rectangle, blur or arbitrary overlap: those can hide pixels while leaving semantic text in the serialized document. Ambiguous clipping, masking and filter geometry is omitted fail-safe, so selection may be lost rather than uncertain content exposed. A purely visual afterRender change does not prove semantics changed; an incompatible change to viewBox, root paint/layout or intrinsic aspect fails instead of guessing coordinates. Where no font is embedded, base-14 fonts encode WinAnsi and other scripts use an invisible Type0 font with a /ToUnicode map, so extraction works for every script whether or not a glyph travels. What the file can paint is the next section. Fonts and vector text Option Default Meaning embedFonts true Embed the capture's @font-face binaries and point the text at them. 'full' embeds unsubsetted; false embeds nothing. vectorText false Paint eligible runs as real vector glyphs instead of leaving them invisible over the raster. Embedded fonts The capture has to CARRY its fonts for the export to embed them: pass embedFonts: true to snapdom(…) (the engine option that inlines @font-face ), and the PDF side reads those rules, fetches each face the text actually painted with, and embeds a subset of it: only the glyphs the document drew, renumbered into a dense space. On a Latin page a ~320 kB face travels as a few kB. A face travels once however many styles and pages use it, and the saving is declared per face. The subset renders pixel-identical to the whole font, which the suite asserts by rendering both through pdf.js. It is fail-safe: a TrueType face it cannot subset falls back to a whole embed with an explicit CIDToGIDMap , never a corrupt glyph. CFF/OpenType ( OTTO ) faces are always embedded whole, so 'full' only differs for TrueType. Per run, an embedded face is used only when its own cmap covers every character of that run; a run it cannot carry falls back to the unembedded layer and is counted. System fonts have no bytes a page can hand over and travel by name as before. WOFF unpacks; WOFF2, TrueType collections and faces whose OS/2 fsType forbids embedding are refused with their reason rather than embedded anyway. Text extraction is byte-for-byte identical with and without embedding, because extraction runs off /ToUnicode either way. Vector text By default the visible text is the raster, which is pixel-exact but still pixels. With vectorText: true the exporter paints eligible runs as real vector glyphs from the embedded fonts, so the type is crisp at any zoom and the file is a fraction of the size. That is a different fidelity model from the pixel-exact capture, and it is opt-in for exactly that reason. A run is painted only where no shaping stands between code points and glyphs: left-to-right, in a covering embedded face, with a resolved colour. RTL, complex scripts, uncovered characters and unresolved colours are not painted, because one CID per code point would place their glyphs wrong. Those runs stay on the raster, and in an image-free export they are invisible and reported. image:false, vectorText:true gives a small, fully vector text PDF. Only text and vector furniture travel; borders, checkboxes, background images and any unpaintable run are absent. Measured, the mega fixture is ~22 kB this way against ~420 kB with the raster. image:true, vectorText:true gives the raster plus crisp glyphs painted over it. Larger, but sharp under magnification. Interior glyph positions follow the embedded font's own advances scaled to the run's measured width ( Tz ), not the browser's kerned positions, so a heavily kerned pair can drift sub-pixel from the raster. Extraction is unchanged. Navigation and tagging Option Default Meaning outline true Capture-time bookmarks from headings; see the lifecycle table. tagged true Structure headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, sections and figures. lang DOM / null PDF document language, for example en or es-MX . The PDF/UA-1 claim is earned, never configured There is no option that asserts conformance. The exporter computes eligibility per export and writes the claim only when all of it holds: every text-showing operation on an embedded face, tagged structure present, a document language, a meta.title to display, and no painted image without alternative text. When it does, the XMP carries pdfuaid:part 1 and the report says so ( report.pdfua === true ). When the fonts are clean but a blocker remains, the export does not claim: it names the blockers, so the fix is a line of configuration or markup rather than a guess. Two blockers to know in advance. Fillable fields block the claim, because their editor-facing /DA types in unembedded Helvetica, so a UA-claiming export pairs with fields: false . A painted or role="img" element with no accessible name blocks it too: give it alt , aria-label or title , or alt="" when it is decorative. Links are tagged as /Link structure elements carrying /OBJR references. Fillable form fields Option Default Meaning fields true Emit measured controls as real AcroForm fields that are fillable, tabbable and extractable. false keeps their values in the invisible text layer instead. A captured form should still be a form. Text inputs, textareas, checkboxes, radio groups and selects become widget annotations carrying their DOM name, value, options and checked state. readonly / disabled map to the read-only flag; required and maxlength travel; and the accessible label ( aria-label ,

text: Export plugins PDF Vector All plugins Vector reference Full API reference Source · MIT All plugin demos Live Vector export Live sample Component SVG illustration Chart Form controls Generate Vector Editable source Generated output Nothing generated yet. Previous Next Copy to Figma Edit the source, then generate a Vector. Code for this demo Build / Plugins / Vector Official plugin · MIT Export editable vector artwork. Reconstruct supported text and shapes as SVG artwork or copy the captured result into Figma. Open source Vector is MIT-licensed source inside packages/plugins/vector . Available in @zumer/snapdom-plugins@4 for SnapDOM 3.x. These demos use the official plugin; npm run site uses your local build. Fidelity See what changes in each format Browsers, SVG and Figma do not support the same effects. The plugin tells you when it had to adapt, rasterize or omit something, and identifies the affected layer. You can review those changes before handing the file to a designer or a client. Exact The destination can reproduce the layer as editable vector content. Adapted The layer remains vector, but an effect was translated to the closest available equivalent. Rasterized or omitted The effect has no usable vector equivalent. The report names the layer and explains what happened. The clearest case is backdrop-filter : frosted glass is a blur of whatever sits behind the panel, and SVG has no way to express that, so the panel arrives as a flat colour. The report names the layer, and the limits list it. Read about fidelity reports How it works Built from the browser's resolved layout Grid, flexbox, sticky positioning and container queries are already resolved on screen. The plugin measures that result instead of trying to implement another CSS layout engine. Editable output Text remains text. Gradients, borders, radii, shadows, transforms, images and DOM hierarchy become vector paint and usable layers. Browser layout Boxes, text lines and baselines are measured from the rendered page, including grid, flexbox, pseudo-elements and open shadow DOM. Private by design The plugin runs in the browser, including authenticated and staging pages. Captures are not uploaded to a server. Tested output 729 checks over 19 fixtures. Fixtures are emitted, rendered and compared against screenshots of the live elements. The whole API Two methods on a SnapDOM capture Register the plugin on a capture and it gains toVector() and toFigma() , alongside toPng() and toCanvas() . The only option is exclude . import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import vector from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/vector' const shot = await snapdom(document.querySelector( '#plan-card' ), { plugins: [vector()] }) const svg = await shot.toVector() // standalone SVG, no foreignObject, text is text await shot.toFigma() // on the clipboard: paste it into Figma Read the reference Where it goes An SVG file, or a paste into Figma Both come from the same capture of the page, and neither needs a server or an install. Flat SVG shot.toVector() Standalone SVG with editable text and native shapes. Open it in Illustrator, Inkscape, Penpot, Figma, a browser, a printer or a plotter. Figma shot.toFigma() Copies the capture in Figma's own paste format. Paste it into a Figma file and you get frames, editable text, gradients, shadows and images, with nothing installed. The format is undocumented, so if a Figma release breaks it, the SVG route keeps working while we update. Open source Included in the SnapDOM monorepo The Vector plugin is available as MIT-licensed source in packages/plugins/vector . PDF and Vector are available on npm in @zumer/snapdom-plugins 4.x and require SnapDOM 3.x. Read the reference · SnapDOM on GitHub Before you ask Questions Is this a tracer? Does it vectorise the pixels? No. Nothing is traced and nothing is recognised. Every box, line and baseline is read from the live layout, and every fill is parsed from the CSS that produced it. A tracer cannot tell you the second stop of a gradient; this hands you its colour and position. Will my page come into Figma perfect? No, and any tool that says otherwise is one you will stop trusting on the third capture. Some things have no Figma equivalent at all: a colour-matrix filter, OpenType feature settings, per-range baseline shift. The difference here is that you get the list, per node, before you paste. Do I need a Figma plugin? No. toFigma() copies the capture and you paste it into Figma. The flat SVG opens in Illustrator, Inkscape, Penpot and any browser too, which is why this is not a Figma product with a lock-in problem. Does anything leave the machine? No. The engine runs in your page, and the copy for Figma goes through your own clipboard. For a lot of teams that is a legal requirement. Which browsers? Chromium today. Everything is measured there and the pixel baselines were recorded there. We have not run it against Firefox or WebKit, so we are not claiming them. What if it does not work for my page? Send us the page. A reproducible case helps improve fidelity, and the samples above are there so you can check the output on pages like yours first.

title: SnapDOM Vector reference
text: SnapDOM Vector A SnapDOM plugin. Register it on a capture and that capture gains toVector() , a standalone SVG, and toFigma() , a copy you paste into Figma. This page is the whole reference. Getting started The Vector plugin and its internal SVD format live in packages/plugins/vector under the MIT license. The plugin package is available on npm in @zumer/snapdom-plugins 4.x and requires SnapDOM 3.x. SnapDOM 3 is a peer dependency; it is not bundled in. import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import vector from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/vector' const shot = await snapdom(document.querySelector( '#plan-card' ), { plugins: [vector()] }) const svg = await shot.toVector() // a standalone SVG string await shot.toFigma() // on the clipboard: paste it into Figma Nothing runs on a server and nothing is uploaded. Everything happens in the page you are already looking at, which is the point: the component worth capturing is usually behind a login. Registering Register it per capture . Registering it globally costs you something, so here are both forms and the reason to prefer the first: // this capture only, and the one to use await snapdom(el, { plugins: [vector()] }) // every capture in the page snapdom.plugins(vector()) A plugin with render hooks suspends SnapDOM's burst optimisation on the captures it runs on, because burst answers with a memoized URL without re-entering the capture pipeline, and then there is no clone for this engine to read. Registered per capture, that cost lands on the captures that asked for it. Registered globally, it lands on all of them, including the toPng() in your hot path. Both methods throw if the captured element has no layout box (an element with display: none has nothing to measure), and if the capture carries no clone, which happens when burst: true was forced on the snapdom() call. Leave burst unset. The captured element must still be connected, with its styles available, when you export. Everything about the capture stays on the snapdom() call. scale , dpr , backgroundColor and the rest are read before the plugin runs, so there is no second set of names for them here. exclude Option Default exclude none A CSS selector, a predicate (element) => boolean , or an array of either. Matching elements and their subtrees are left out of the vector output, text and layer names included. It is the only option. Give it to vector({ exclude }) as the default for every export from that capture, or to a single toVector() or toFigma() call, where it wins for that call. const shot = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [vector({ exclude: '.no-print' })] }) const svg = await shot.toVector({ exclude: [ '.no-print' , (node) => node.dataset.private === 'true' ] }) SnapDOM's own exclude on the snapdom() call also applies: anything it leaves out of the capture never reaches the vector output. toVector() shot.toVector(options?) → Promise <string> A standalone SVG string. No foreignObject , anywhere. An SVG with a foreignObject in it is an HTML document wearing an SVG hat, and every vector tool opens it empty. Here a rectangle is a <rect> and a line of text is a <text> . The file opens in Illustrator, Inkscape, Penpot, Figma and any browser. The browser breaks the lines and the SVG only draws them. A block that occupies more than one line becomes one <text> per visual line, each at its measured baseline, so no editor re-wraps your paragraph differently. Gradients, borders, radii, shadows, transforms, clips and images become native SVG paint. -webkit-text-stroke is a real stroke, and background-clip: text becomes the text's own fill. textLength is written only when a font binary travels with the file. Pinning a line to a width measured with your font, in a viewer that substituted another one, squeezes the glyphs. Native form controls are reconstructed at Chromium's measured proportions from their kind, state and accent colour, and each one is declared as a reconstruction. The file is self-describing : the approximations are written into an XML comment under the <svg> tag, so a file that travels without its report cannot exist. toFigma() shot.toFigma(options?) → Promise <void> Puts the capture on the clipboard in Figma's own paste format. Paste into a Figma file and you get frames, editable text, gradients, shadows, borders and images, with nothing installed. It resolves once the clipboard holds the copy. button.addEventListener( 'click' , async () => { await shot.toFigma() toast( 'Copied. Paste it into Figma.' ) }) Call it from a user action, on https or localhost. It uses the async clipboard API, and browsers only let a page the user is interacting with write to the clipboard. Outside a secure context it rejects with a message that says so. letter-spacing survives , which Figma's SVG importer cannot do: measured, a 376.8px line of text arrives at 449px through the SVG route, 50px of that from ignored tracking. Nodes whose paint the paste format cannot spell are drawn as vector artwork and carried as an image, unless they hold text, which stays editable. Effects that read what is underneath a node ( mix-blend-mode , backdrop-filter ) arrive unblended. The format is Figma's, and it is undocumented. Figma can change it in any release, with no error; the only symptom is a paste that does nothing. If that happens, toVector() and Figma's SVG import keep working while we update. Diagnostics Every approximation (a conic gradient drawn as wedges, a shadow spread folded into a blur, a filter a destination cannot run) is printed to the console under [snapdom-vector] , grouped by code with a count and up to three distinct messages, so four hundred identical warnings come out as one line and a count. The codes are stable and greppable, and toVector() also writes the list into the SVG. A diagnostic that says something will be lost in the destination (the SVG is exactly right in a browser, and Figma runs only part of it) is a warning about where the file is going, not a degradation of the file. What reaches the output, and what does not The engine walks the clone SnapDOM already resolved, which is why membership in the tree is not an argument here. In: Pseudo-elements ( ::before , ::after , ::first-letter ) as real nodes with real boxes, with counters and quotes resolved. Shadow DOM , flattened, so slotted content appears once, at the slot. Icon fonts resolved by ligature, and inline <svg> carried as vector with its element ids namespaced per instance. Images from currentSrc , so srcset resolves to what was actually shown, with object-fit and object-position applied. An SVG source is inlined as vector, not rasterized. Scroll offsets , applied, and overflow clipping as a real clip. <canvas> and <video> , as bitmaps. A tainted canvas is omitted with a reason rather than throwing. In-flight animations , at the values of the frame that was captured. Out: Anything exclude named, and anything SnapDOM itself excludes. display: none , visibility: hidden , and content clipped away by an overflow ancestor. The value inside a native control. The text in an <input> , the chosen <option> of a <select> and a placeholder are painted by the browser itself and no CSS property describes them. The widget's frame, border and background are drawn. Cross-origin iframes. The frame becomes a placeholder. Closed shadow roots , which are unreadable by anyone. Limits Written down because you will meet them, and meeting them here is better than meeting them in front of a client. Chromium. Everything is measured there and the pixel baselines were recorded there. Other engines are not tested, and we do not claim them. No font binary travels. The output names the family and the face; it does not embed the file. So a viewer without your font substitutes one. A system font keyword is not a font name. Text painted by -apple-system or system-ui cannot tell any destination which face to load. Auto Layout is not inferred. Everything lands positioned. A frame you can move is not a frame that reflows, and guessing wrong at the layout is worse than not guessing. backdrop-filter does not survive. Frosted glass is a blur of whatever sits behind the panel, and neither SVG nor Figma can say that about an arbitrary backdrop. The panel arrives as a flat colour, and the diagnostics name it. A conic gradient becomes 128 flat wedges plus a small disc capping the apex. SVG has no conic paint server. Shadow spread is approximate. feMorphology 's kernel is rectangular, so the spread corners are. 3D transforms are flattened to their 2D projection, with a diagnostic. Figma has no colour-matrix effect , so filter: saturate(…) and its relatives have no equivalent there. They are named, with the CSS verbatim, rather than dropped quietly. The capture is one subtree, one viewport, one moment. No page-wide capture, no responsive variants, no component variants inferred from a static picture. Something here wrong or missing? Tell us . The documentation is part of what you bought.

title: SnapDOM Documentation — API, Options, Plugins & Cache
text: ⌕ Getting started Overview Capture API API reference Cache and preCapture Options Options Plugins Plugin API Docs / Getting started / Overview Documentation SnapDOM Documentation Capture a DOM element once, then export it as an image, PDF, vector or recording. This reference covers SnapDOM 3. Quick start API reference What is SnapDOM SnapDOM is a high-performance DOM engine that captures a rendered element in the browser. One capture becomes SVG, PNG, JPG, WebP, canvas or a Blob, with its geometry. Plugins add paginated PDF, editable vector, HTML, text or JSON context and element maps from that state, or record new captures as GIF or video. Documentation sections API reference: methods & exporters Options: every capture option Plugins: extend the pipeline Cache & preCapture: performance Quick start Capture any DOM element to PNG in one line: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; const img = await snapdom.toPng(document.querySelector('#card')); document.body.appendChild(img); Reusable capture (one clone, multiple exports): const result = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#card')); await result.toPng(); // → HTMLImageElement await result.toSvg(); // → SVG as Image await result.download({ format: 'jpg', filename: 'card.jpg' }); Installation NPM / Yarn npm i @zumer/snapdom@latest yarn add @zumer/snapdom@latest CDN <!-- Minified build --> <script src="https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.js"></script> <!-- Minified ES Module build --> <script type="module"> import { snapdom } from "https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.mjs"; </script> Build outputs Variant File Use case ESM (tree-shakeable) dist/snapdom.mjs Bundlers (Vite, webpack), import IIFE (global) dist/snapdom.js Browser script tag; exposes window.snapdom . No CommonJS build. Plugin registry import. The subpath shares the core runtime and registry: import { registerPlugins } from '@zumer/snapdom/plugins'; Capture flow A capture freezes the subtree; exports read that state. The steps: Stage What happens Clone Deep clone with styles, Shadow DOM, iframes. Leave nodes out with exclude . Styles & Pseudo Inline ::before / ::after as elements, resolve counter() / counters() . Images & Backgrounds Fetch and inline external images/backgrounds as data URLs. Fonts Embed the webfonts the capture uses by default. Render icon-font glyphs through the icon path. SVG Wrap clone in <foreignObject> , serialize to data:image/svg+xml . Export Return the SVG, rasterize to PNG/JPG/WebP/canvas, create a blob, or run a plugin export. Plugins can use the clone without rendering by declaring needs: 'clone' . Image exports require 'render' , the default. Hooks and custom outputs: see the plugins guide . Usage patterns Pattern When to use snapdom(el) Reusable — one clone many exports (PNG + JPG + download). snapdom.toPng(el) Shortcut — single export, less code. Every method is in the API reference ; everything you can pass is in the options reference . Choose a recipe for your output For a PNG preview, a downloaded file or a Blob to upload, use the HTML to PNG recipe . For a shareable report with several charts, use the dashboard export recipe . Keep the component in place while capturing; the library exports the DOM your users already see. For framework state updates, the Angular guide waits for the next render, the Svelte guide waits for tick() , and the Lit guide selects a card inside its shadow root after updateComplete .
