title: Claude Code capture skill: visual checks without Playwright
text: ⌕ Overview All posts Posts PDF vs html2canvas + jsPDF Claude Code capture skill Editable SVG and Figma SnapDOM v3 is out DOM capture boundaries Tiled rasterization Painting without a canvas Blog / Posts / Claude Code capture skill Agents · Tutorial Claude Code capture skill: visual checks without writing Playwright scripts A downloadable Claude Code skill and billing-card fixture. Route app capture to SnapEye, visual review to SnapDIFF and browser interaction to SnapSurf. Capture before editing, compare afterward The skill below tells Claude Code which component to capture, when to save the baseline and how to read the comparison. SnapEye handles local app capture, SnapDIFF visual review, SnapSurf browser interaction. None of this needs a Playwright test script. SnapSurf uses Playwright internally to control its browser; SnapEye captures through the running app; SnapDIFF compares captures inside the page. SnapEye, SnapDIFF and SnapSurf have different roles SnapEye: capture your app and compare before and after Claude runs a command to capture a component in your local app. After a code change, another command compares it with the saved image and reports whether the pixels changed. Good for checking a CSS refactor or finding a visual regression. SnapEye captures and records the app; it does not click through the interface. SnapDIFF: review visual differences inside the browser SnapDIFF captures components, compares them with saved images and shows the differences in the page, where you inspect and approve changes through its reporter. Use it for interactive review. Its basic browser workflow saves references in that browser’s storage; blocking a CI build needs the separate test setup. SnapSurf: let the agent operate the browser SnapSurf lets Claude open a page, find a control, click or type, and check what changed: open a settings form, verify that a dialog appeared. Use it when the task needs interaction. It starts its own browser session, without the logins from your open Chrome tabs. Semantic verification says whether the interface changed state; visual comparison says whether captured pixels changed. A “saved” message can be correct while a button overlaps it, so check pixels when the task concerns appearance. Set up local capture in a Vite app npm install --save-dev @zumer/snapeye @zumer/snapdom@3 import { defineConfig } from 'vite'; import { snapeye } from '@zumer/snapeye/vite'; export default defineConfig({ plugins: [snapeye()] }); Start the dev server, then capture the component before editing it, with a stable viewport, fixed fixture data and a specific target rather than the whole application. npx snapeye capture billing-card-desktop --target '#billing-card' # Close the capture-trigger tab before editing, then: npx snapeye diff billing-card-desktop --target '#billing-card' --fail-on-change Read status first. A successful run with diff.changed: false passes an appearance-preserving refactor. If it changed, inspect the reported regions and artifacts. An environment failure is not a passing comparison. Download a Claude Code capture skill Save this complete SKILL.md as .claude/skills/visual-capture/SKILL.md in the project. The skill supplies the routing instructions; the tools, installed separately, perform the capture. The official skill guide documents the directory and frontmatter. --- name: visual-capture description: Capture and verify local UI changes with SnapEye; use SnapSurf for browser interactions and SnapDIFF for in-page review. --- Capture the baseline before editing. Keep the viewport and fixture data fixed. Use SnapEye for a selector-level capture and read status before diff.changed. Never replace a baseline simply to hide a regression. Use SnapSurf for navigation and verify after every action. Report the target, artifacts, tool versions and what was actually verified. The downloadable version also covers errors, intentional visual changes and signed-in sessions, and keeps publication and baseline approval subject to the user’s instructions. A reproducible billing-card exercise Open the fixture or download its HTML : a static card with synthetic data and a button that deliberately changes its border, so baseline and regression are easy to tell apart. npm install --save-dev vite @zumer/snapeye @zumer/snapdom@3 npx snapeye serve billing-card.html # In another terminal, using the URL printed by serve: npx snapeye capture billing-card --url <printed-url> --target '#billing-card' # Close the capture-trigger tab, edit the CSS, then compare: npx snapeye diff billing-card --url <printed-url> --target '#billing-card' --fail-on-change For an interaction-only state, a fresh trigger URL reloads the page. Reach the state with a browser tool and use SnapEye's documented in-page API; the CLI will not have captured an already-open modal. The SnapDIFF live demos show an in-page review workflow with deliberate visual drift. Add browser interaction through MCP SnapSurf is published in the official MCP Registry as io.github.zumerlab/snapsurf and listed in Glama . The registry entry checked on October 5, 2026 is version 0.1.2, distributed as the npm package @zumer/snapsurf . claude mcp add --scope user snapsurf -- npx -y -p @zumer/snapsurf@latest snapsurf-mcp Then ask Claude to open the app, find a named control, act, verify and assert the intended transition. Read structuredContent , get fresh target ids after new observations, and escalate to pixels when the semantic report cannot answer the question. A semantic diff does not prove a SnapDOM image has the right pixels. For a workflow that needs the user's existing signed-in tab, use an authorized integration for that tab. A useful task to give Claude “Refactor the billing card CSS without changing its appearance. Capture #billing-card before editing, keep the fixture and viewport fixed, compare afterward, and report the JSON verdict and artifact paths. If verification fails, explain the failure; do not overwrite the reference.” For an intentional redesign, specify which region may change and inspect it before approving a new reference. Keep the original reference until that review is done. Related: element capture , recapture and invalidation , React lifecycle timing . Sources checked October 5, 2026: SnapEye setup and CLI , SnapDIFF workflows , SnapSurf MCP integration , and the Claude Code skill guide above. Playwright MCP, for comparison Microsoft’s Playwright MCP also lets an agent operate a browser without a standalone test script; its documented approach uses structured accessibility snapshots. SnapSurf adds a digest-and-diff workflow with assertions over retained transitions. Both control a browser, so compare their observation and verification APIs against the task at hand. Keep Playwright tests for an established end-to-end suite, multi-browser automation or a CI workflow your team already maintains. Add selector-level DOM capture when the immediate question is what changed in a running component. Protect the baseline during hot reload After a CLI capture finishes, close its trigger tab or navigate to the ordinary app URL before editing. In our local SnapEye 0.4.0 fixture, leaving the capture query open during Vite hot reload triggered another capture and replaced the baseline, which would turn a real change into a misleading no-change verdict. With the capture URL removed before editing, the deliberate border change produced changed: true and exit code 3. The fixture was checked in Chromium at 320 × 240 captured CSS pixels. An unchanged run reported zero changed pixels; the border regression reported a change. The check covered this fixture in Chromium only. title: How to Screenshot a Div in JavaScript — SnapDOM
text: ⌕ Overview How to capture the DOM Basics Screenshot a div Convert HTML to PNG Convert HTML to SVG Render HTML to Canvas Capture in high resolution Real content Export a dashboard Export a React component Export an invoice Generate a social card Capture before a PDF Export a chart as SVG Save a Chart.js chart Special cases Capture without Puppeteer Capture Shadow DOM Capture a full page Capture an iframe Visual regression Frameworks React Vue Next.js Svelte Angular Lit How-to / Basics / Screenshot a div How-To Recipe How to screenshot a div in JavaScript Select the rendered element, call snapdom.toPng , and use the returned image in a preview or download. TL;DR const img = await snapdom.toPng(document.querySelector('#my-div')); is the entire recipe. The promise resolves to an HTMLImageElement you can append, download or upload. Step 1: Install SnapDOM npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest If you don't use a bundler, you can also use the CDN build: < script type= "module" > import { snapdom } from "https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.mjs" ; </ script > Step 2: Pick the div you want to screenshot Anything that's part of the live document tree works. Most people use document.querySelector : const el = document. querySelector ( '#card' ); It doesn't need to be inside the viewport, but it must be attached to the document and not display: none . If it loads web fonts or images, wait for them first: await document.fonts.ready; await Promise.all(Array.from(el.querySelectorAll('img'), img => img.decode())); For an iframe or a web component, see the iframe and Shadow DOM recipes. Step 3: Capture it One line: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; const img = await snapdom. toPng (el); The returned img is a real HTMLImageElement with the captured content as its src (a PNG data URL). Step 4: Do something with the image Append it to the page const img = await snapdom. toPng (el); document.body. appendChild (img); Download it as a file const result = await snapdom (el); await result. download ({ format: 'png' , filename: 'card' }); Get a Blob to upload to a server const blob = await snapdom. toBlob (el, { format: 'png' }); const form = new FormData (); form. append ( 'file' , blob, 'screenshot.png' ); await fetch ( '/api/upload' , { method: 'POST' , body: form }); Full working example Drop this into a fresh HTML file and open it in a browser: <! DOCTYPE html > < html > < body > < div id= "card" style= "padding:24px;background:#4f46e5;color:#fff;border-radius:12px;" > < h2 > Hello SnapDOM </ h2 > < p > This entire div is about to become a PNG. </ p > </ div > < button id= "go" > Capture </ button > < script type= "module" > import { snapdom } from "https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.mjs" ; document. getElementById ( 'go' ). addEventListener ( 'click' , async () => { const img = await snapdom. toPng (document. getElementById ( 'card' )); document.body. appendChild (img); }); </ script > </ body > </ html > Or try it right here The example above, running on this page — same div, same snapdom.toPng call: Hello SnapDOM This entire div is about to become a PNG. Capture Download The captured PNG will appear here. Useful options dpr: 2 — pixel density (auto-detects window.devicePixelRatio for retina; override here when you need a fixed value). scale: 2 — multiply the captured size (zoom). Different from dpr : scale makes the output bigger, dpr makes it sharper at the same logical size. backgroundColor: '#fff' — fill transparent areas with a colour. embedFonts: 'auto' — the v3 default embeds used web fonts. exclude: ['.skip'] — skip any element matching the selector. useProxy: 'https://your-proxy.example.com/' — fetch cross-origin images through a CORS proxy. Frequently asked questions Why not use the browser's built-in screenshot API? There isn't one. The closest thing is the Screen Capture API ( getDisplayMedia ) which captures the whole tab or screen and requires user permission — it cannot target a specific DOM element. SnapDOM is the workaround. Does this work with web fonts? Yes. SnapDOM embeds used web fonts by default with embedFonts: 'auto' , provided their files are accessible. title: How to Save a Chart.js Chart as a PNG — SnapDOM
text: ⌕ Overview How to capture the DOM Basics Screenshot a div Convert HTML to PNG Convert HTML to SVG Render HTML to Canvas Capture in high resolution Real content Export a dashboard Export a React component Export an invoice Generate a social card Capture before a PDF Export a chart as SVG Save a Chart.js chart Special cases Capture without Puppeteer Capture Shadow DOM Capture a full page Capture an iframe Visual regression Frameworks React Vue Next.js Svelte Angular Lit How-to / Real content / Save a Chart.js chart How-To Recipe How to save a Chart.js chart as a PNG Chart.js draws to a <canvas> , so its built-in toBase64Image() exports the chart canvas, including its built-in labels. When you want the title, HTML legend and container in the picture too, capture the whole component with SnapDOM. TL;DR Wrap the chart, wait for it to finish drawing, then const img = await snapdom.toPng(wrapper) . You get one PNG with the canvas and everything around it. The problem Chart.js renders inside a <canvas> element. Its native chart.toBase64Image() exports exactly that canvas and drops anything you laid out in HTML around it: a heading, a custom legend, annotations, the card background. If your export needs to look like the chart your users actually see on the page, you need to capture the surrounding DOM as well. SnapDOM captures a DOM subtree — including live <canvas> pixels — into a single image, so the chart and its frame come out as one composited PNG. Step 1: Install npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest chart.js Without a bundler, load both from a CDN: import { snapdom } from "https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.mjs" ; import Chart from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/chart.js/auto/+esm" ; Step 2: Wrap the chart in a capture target Put the canvas inside an element that also holds whatever you want in the exported image: < div id= "chart-card" style= "padding:20px;background:#fff;border-radius:12px;" > < h3 > Monthly revenue </ h3 > < canvas id= "chart" ></ canvas > </ div > Step 3: Wait for the draw, then capture A canvas only holds pixels once Chart.js has painted them. Capturing during the entry animation gives you a blank or half-drawn plot. The reliable fix is to capture from the animation's onComplete callback: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; import Chart from 'chart.js/auto' ; const chart = new Chart (document. getElementById ( 'chart' ), { type: 'bar' , data: { labels: [ 'Jan' , 'Feb' , 'Mar' , 'Apr' ], datasets: [{ label: 'Revenue' , data: [12, 19, 9, 22] }] }, options: { animation: { onComplete : async () => { const img = await snapdom. toPng (document. getElementById ( 'chart-card' )); document.body. appendChild (img); } } } }); Prefer a static export with no timing games? Set options.animation = false and capture right after new Chart(...) returns. Step 4: Download it as a file const result = await snapdom (document. getElementById ( 'chart-card' )); await result. download ({ format: 'png' , filename: 'revenue-chart' }); Or get a Blob to upload: const blob = await snapdom. toBlob (document. getElementById ( 'chart-card' ), { format: 'png' }); Expected result A single PNG that matches what's on screen: the <h3> heading, the card's white background and rounded corners, and the fully rendered bar chart — all in one image at your device pixel ratio. Pass { scale: 2 } to toPng for a sharper, higher-resolution export. Try it live A real Chart.js bar chart, in a card with an HTML heading. Capture it and compare: the exported PNG includes the heading and the card frame — exactly what toBase64Image() would drop: Monthly revenue Capture chart card Download The captured PNG will appear here. Going further Capture the wrapper when you need the chart together with surrounding HTML labels and card styling. For an animation, the optional GIF export plugin can capture a sequence of frames; see the plugins page . Frequently asked questions My exported chart is blank — why? You captured before Chart.js finished drawing. Capture inside options.animation.onComplete , or set options.animation = false so the chart paints synchronously. Can I export just the canvas without the surrounding HTML? Use chart.toBase64Image() when the canvas alone is the output you need, including Chart.js titles or legends drawn inside it. Capture the wrapper with SnapDOM when you also need surrounding HTML, custom legends or container styling. How do I get a higher-resolution image? Pass { scale: 2 } (or higher) to snapdom.toPng . SnapDOM also respects window.devicePixelRatio automatically. Does this work with react-chartjs-2? Yes. Put a ref on the wrapping element and call snapdom.toPng(ref.current) from the chart's onComplete option. The wrapper is just a DOM node — SnapDOM doesn't care how it was rendered. Step 1: Install npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest Or load it from a CDN if you don't use a bundler: < script type= "module" > import { snapdom } from "https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.mjs" ; </ script > Pattern 1: Append the PNG to the page Useful for quick previews and demos. snapdom.toPng returns an HTMLImageElement , ready to insert anywhere in the DOM: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; const img = await snapdom. toPng (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); document.body. appendChild (img); Pattern 2: Download the PNG as a file SnapDOM ships with a one-liner that triggers the browser's download flow: const result = await snapdom (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); await result. download ({ format: 'png' , filename: 'card' }); If you need more control, build the download yourself with a Blob and an anchor tag: const blob = await snapdom. toBlob (document. querySelector ( '#card' ), { format: 'png' }); const url = URL. createObjectURL (blob); const a = document. createElement ( 'a' ); a.href = url; a.download = 'card.png' ; a. click (); URL. revokeObjectURL (url); Pattern 3: Upload the PNG to a server Capture the element to a Blob, wrap it in FormData , and POST it to your endpoint: const blob = await snapdom. toBlob (document. querySelector ( '#card' ), { format: 'png' }); const form = new FormData (); form. append ( 'file' , blob, 'card.png' ); const response = await fetch ( '/api/upload' , { method: 'POST' , body: form, }); const { url } = await response. json (); console . log ( 'Uploaded to' , url); This is the same pattern you'd use to generate dynamic og:image share cards — capture the rendered card client-side, upload to a CDN, return the URL. Try the three patterns live Same element, three buttons: append the PNG, download it, or produce the upload-ready Blob: HTML PNG Gradients, borders & shadows Rounded corners, a dashed border, a gradient, ready to capture together. ⚡ Even this shadow Append PNG Download Get Blob The result will appear here. Bonus: Get a Base64 / data URL If you specifically need a base64 string (e.g. to email or embed inline), call toPng and read the src of the returned image: const img = await snapdom. toPng (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); const dataUrl = img.src; // "data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo…" High-DPI / retina output SnapDOM picks up the device's devicePixelRatio automatically through the dpr option, so retina screens already get sharp output without configuration. Override it with dpr when you want a fixed pixel density (e.g. exporting a 2× asset on a non-retina machine): const img = await snapdom. toPng (el, { dpr: 2 }); scale multiplies the captured size when no explicit width or height is set. Use scale when you want a larger image; use dpr when you want the same logical size at higher pixel density. They can be combined: const img = await snapdom. toPng (el, { dpr: 2 , // retina pixel density scale: 1.5 , // zoom 1.5× backgroundColor: '#ffffff' , }); Frequently asked questions Can I convert HTML to PNG without a server? Yes. SnapDOM runs in the browser and does not need a screenshot server. Its SVG foreignObject pipeline uses the browser's renderer; fonts and images may still require network requests. What if I need JPG or WebP instead of PNG? Use snapdom.toJpg(el, { quality: 0.9 }) or snapdom.toWebp(el, { quality: 0.9 }) . The API surface is identical, only the output format changes. How do I render custom fonts correctly? SnapDOM defaults to embedFonts: 'auto' , which embeds used web fonts when their files are accessible. Use localFonts or excludeFonts when you need more control. Can I exclude some elements from the capture? Yes. Pass { exclude: ['.skip-me'] } with a list of CSS selectors, or { exclude: node => … } for a predicate that returns true for nodes to omit. What about converting HTML to PDF? Use the MIT pdf plugin. Its toPdf() method returns a PDF Blob with selectable text, pagination and links. The plugin is available on npm in @zumer/snapdom-plugins 4.x; see the PDF reference for installation and examples. Does it handle Shadow DOM and Web Components? Open shadow roots need no extra setup. See Capture Shadow DOM . TL;DR Wait for this.updateComplete , select the card from this.renderRoot , then export it. SnapDOM can walk open shadow roots; document.querySelector cannot reach their internal nodes. Install and use SnapDOM in Lit Install the capture library in your existing Lit project: npm install @zumer/snapdom Load this module in your client entry, then place in your page. import { LitElement, html, css } from 'lit' import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' class ExportCard extends LitElement { static properties = { title: { type: String }, saving: { state: true }, error: { state: true }, } static styles = css` article { padding: 24px; background: #eef3ff; border-radius: 12px; } ` constructor() { super() this.title = 'Monthly report' this.saving = false this.error = '' } async save() { this.saving = true this.error = '' try { await this.updateComplete const card = this.renderRoot.querySelector('#card') await document.fonts.ready await Promise.all(Array.from(card.querySelectorAll('img'), img => img.decode())) await snapdom.download(card, { format: 'png', filename: 'lit-card' }) } catch (cause) { this.error = cause instanceof Error ? cause.message : 'Capture failed' } finally { this.saving = false } } render() { return html`

${this.title}

Ready to share.

${this.error}

` } } customElements.define('export-card', ExportCard) Wait for the right Lit element updateComplete resolves after this element finishes its update. It does not promise that every nested Lit component or asynchronous resource is ready. If a known child owns part of the report, await that child’s updateComplete before capture too: await this.updateComplete const chart = this.renderRoot.querySelector('report-chart') await chart.updateComplete await snapdom.download(this.renderRoot.querySelector('#card'), { format: 'png' }) For third-party charts, use their documented ready signal. Do not add a fixed timeout and assume the subtree has settled. Choose the host or the internal card Capturing this exports the custom element host, including its open shadow tree and host-level styles. Capturing this.renderRoot.querySelector('#card') exports only the card, leaving the form controls out of the image. The example uses the latter. A closed shadow root is inaccessible to code outside the component. Keep capture inside the component, where the render root reference is available, or provide an explicit export method. SnapDOM cannot bypass that browser boundary. See the Shadow DOM capture recipe for the open-root case. Assets and server-rendered Lit Lit’s update lifecycle does not wait for fonts or image downloads; the example waits for those resources explicitly and reports failures. If a child contains a same-origin iframe, also wait for the frame to load and use the iframe capture recipe . In a server-rendered application, invoke the export after the browser has upgraded and hydrated the relevant components. Run this module in the client entry and capture from an interaction, rather than from the server rendering pipeline. Frequently asked questions Why can document.querySelector not find my card? The card is inside the component’s shadow root. Select it with this.renderRoot.querySelector from the component, or capture the host to include its open shadow tree. Does updateComplete include child updates? Not by default. Wait for known child components’ updateComplete promises and for any separate data or asset readiness signals before capture. TL;DR Bind a template ref with ref="cardRef" , install @zumer/snapdom , and call snapdom.toPng(cardRef.value) from a button handler. SnapDOM returns an HTMLImageElement ready to append. 1. Install npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest Zero runtime dependencies and an ES module entry. In Nuxt, keep imports and capture calls inside the browser boundary. 2. Minimal capture component (Composition API) < script setup > import { ref } from 'vue' ; import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; const cardRef = ref ( null ); async function capture () { if (!cardRef.value) return ; const img = await snapdom. toPng (cardRef.value, { scale: 2 }); document.body. appendChild (img); } < template > < div > < div ref= "cardRef" class= "card" > < h3 > Hello SnapDOM < p > This whole div will be captured. < button @click= "capture" > Capture That's the entire component. The template ref name ( cardRef ) must match the variable declared in the script setup. Try it live This is the component above, running on this page. The button fires snapdom.toPng(cardRef.value) and the captured PNG appears below. SnapDOM only sees the DOM node, so the call is identical whether Vue, React or plain HTML rendered it. Hello SnapDOM This whole div will be captured. Capture Download The captured PNG will appear here. 3. Download instead of appending async function download () { if (!cardRef.value) return ; const result = await snapdom (cardRef.value); await result. download ({ format: 'png' , filename: 'card' }); } 4. Render a live preview Capture to a Blob and create an object URL to use as the preview source: < script setup > import { ref } from 'vue' ; import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; const cardRef = ref ( null ); const previewUrl = ref ( '' ); async function capture () { if (!cardRef.value) return ; const blob = await snapdom. toBlob (cardRef.value, { format: 'png' }); previewUrl.value = URL. createObjectURL (blob); } < template > < div ref= "cardRef" > … < button @click= "capture" > Capture < img v-if= "previewUrl" :src= "previewUrl" alt= "preview" / > Revoke the object URL with URL.revokeObjectURL(previewUrl.value) when you're done with it to avoid leaks. 5. Reusable composable // useSnapdom.js import { ref } from 'vue' ; import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; export function useSnapdom (options = {}) { const target = ref ( null ); async function capture (format = 'png' ) { if (!target.value) return null ; const result = await snapdom (target.value, options); return result. to (format); } return { target, capture }; } < script setup > import { useSnapdom } from './useSnapdom' ; const { target, capture } = useSnapdom ({ scale: 2 , embedFonts: true }); < template > < div ref= "target" > … < button @click= "capture('png')" > Capture Choose the Vue export target Keep the ref on the visible card, invoice or dashboard, and keep the export controls outside that root. Use the invoice export recipe for a printable report or the dashboard recipe for several widgets. After nextTick() and asset readiness, the PNG Blob recipe provides a file for your upload endpoint. Common gotchas The captured image is blank Make sure you trigger the capture from a user event (click) or inside onMounted — never directly inside setup() . The element ref is only assigned after the component has been mounted. Also confirm the captured element isn't v-if 'd off the page. SnapDOM needs the element to be in the live DOM tree. Web fonts aren't being captured SnapDOM defaults to embedFonts: 'auto' and embeds used web fonts when their files are accessible. Wait for application data and fonts to settle before capture if they can change the layout. How do I use SnapDOM with the Options API? Bind ref="cardRef" in the template and access this.$refs.cardRef in a method: const img = await snapdom.toPng(this.$refs.cardRef); Does SnapDOM work with Nuxt? Yes — but only on the client side. Wrap your capture component in or import SnapDOM dynamically inside onMounted so it never runs on the server. Cross-origin images don't render Use the useProxy option pointing to a CORS proxy: { useProxy: 'https://your-proxy.example.com/' } . TL;DR Use viewChild.required to select the rendered card and afterNextRender to capture after signal updates reach the DOM. Keep the export button outside the captured element. Install and use SnapDOM in Angular Install the capture library in your existing Angular project: npm install @zumer/snapdom Add this standalone component to your Angular view. import { Component, ElementRef, Injector, afterNextRender, inject, signal, viewChild } from '@angular/core' import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' @Component({ selector: 'app-export-card', standalone: true, template: `

{{ title() }}

Ready to share.

{{ error() }}

`, }) export class ExportCardComponent { card = viewChild.required>('card') title = signal('Monthly report') saving = signal(false) error = signal('') private injector = inject(Injector) save() { this.saving.set(true) this.error.set('') afterNextRender(async () => { try { const el = this.card().nativeElement await document.fonts.ready await Promise.all(Array.from(el.querySelectorAll('img'), img => img.decode())) await snapdom.download(el, { format: 'png', filename: 'angular-card' }) } catch (error) { this.error.set(error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'Capture failed') } finally { this.saving.set(false) } }, { injector: this.injector }) } } Wait for Angular’s next render The click handler may change signals, fetch data or reveal an @if block. Reading the DOM immediately after that change can capture the previous view. Angular’s afterNextRender callback runs after the next application render; pass the component’s injector when registering it from an event handler. The example’s saving signal schedules that render. An optional viewChild can be undefined when its element is absent; use a required query only for a card that is always rendered. If the card is conditional, wait until it exists before enabling export. Wait for data, images and fonts Finish the application’s data request before scheduling capture. afterNextRender waits for Angular’s DOM work, not network responses. The example then waits for document.fonts.ready and decodes images inside the card; a broken image reaches the status message instead of silently producing an incomplete report. For an exportable chart, wait for its own animation or ready event too. When the output is destined for an upload instead of a download, follow the PNG Blob and FormData pattern . Angular SSR and hydration Keep the export attached to a browser click. Render callbacks do not run during server-side rendering, and a server cannot provide the live layout that SnapDOM captures. For a hydrated application, wait until the component is interactive and its data has settled; a render callback alone is not a blanket guarantee that every child has completed hydration. Frequently asked questions Why does the PNG show the previous signal value? The capture ran before Angular applied the signal change to the DOM. Register afterNextRender with the component injector, then capture from its callback. Can I capture an Angular component on the server? This recipe captures a view in the browser after it becomes interactive. Server-side screenshot jobs need a browser automation tool to load and render the route first. title: Capture HTML to PNG in Next.js with SnapDOM
text: ⌕ Overview How to capture the DOM Basics Screenshot a div Convert HTML to PNG Convert HTML to SVG Render HTML to Canvas Capture in high resolution Real content Export a dashboard Export a React component Export an invoice Generate a social card Capture before a PDF Export a chart as SVG Save a Chart.js chart Special cases Capture without Puppeteer Capture Shadow DOM Capture a full page Capture an iframe Visual regression Frameworks React Vue Next.js Svelte Angular Lit How-to / Frameworks / Next.js Next.js Guide Capture HTML to PNG in Next.js A copy-paste client component for the app router, the SSR pitfall to avoid, and a dynamic import pattern that keeps your bundle small. TL;DR SnapDOM needs a browser DOM. Use a client component for the ref and event handler, then import SnapDOM inside the handler. This keeps capture code out of server rendering. 1. Install npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest Run the capture in a browser event handler after the component has hydrated. 2. App Router: client component Create a client component that owns the ref and capture logic. 'use client' defines a client boundary, but client components may still be prerendered. Importing SnapDOM inside the click handler keeps that import in the browser. // app/capture/CaptureCard.tsx 'use client' ; import { useRef } from 'react' ; export default function CaptureCard () { const cardRef = useRef <HTMLDivElement>( null ); async function handleCapture () { if (!cardRef.current) return ; const { snapdom } = await import ( '@zumer/snapdom' ); const img = await snapdom. toPng (cardRef.current, { scale: 2 }); document.body. appendChild (img); } return ( < div > < div ref={cardRef} className= "card" > < h3 >Hello SnapDOM</ h3 > < p >Captured from a Next.js client component.</ p > </ div > < button onClick={handleCapture}>Capture</ button > </ div > ); } Try it live This is what CaptureCard does after hydration, running on this page. The button fires snapdom.toPng(cardRef.current) and the captured PNG appears below — all client-side, exactly like it will in your Next.js app. Hello SnapDOM Captured from a Next.js client component. Capture Download The captured PNG will appear here. 3. Use it from a server page Server components can render this client component as a child. The 'use client' boundary allows its event handler and ref; the dynamic import inside the handler runs when the user captures: // app/capture/page.tsx import CaptureCard from './CaptureCard' ; export default function Page () { return ( < main > < h1 >SnapDOM in Next.js</ h1 > < CaptureCard /> </ main > ); } 4. Alternative: dynamic import (lazy load) The handler above already loads SnapDOM on demand. You can also load the entire capture component dynamically with SSR disabled. Put this dynamic() call inside a client component: // app/capture/CaptureLazy.tsx 'use client' ; import dynamic from 'next/dynamic' ; export const CaptureCard = dynamic (() => import ( './CaptureCard' ), { ssr: false , loading: () => < p >Loading capture tool…</ p >, }); Your server page then imports CaptureCard from this wrapper. In the pages router ( pages/capture.tsx ) there's no 'use client' directive and no restriction — ssr: false works directly in the page file. 5. Bonus: dynamic OG / share images Generate share cards on the fly when the user clicks "share". Capture the rendered card to a Blob, upload it to your CDN, and use that URL as the og:image for the share link: async function share () { if (!cardRef.current) return ; const { snapdom } = await import('@zumer/snapdom'); const blob = await snapdom. toBlob (cardRef.current, { scale: 2 , format: 'png' }); const form = new FormData (); form. append ( 'file' , blob, 'share.png' ); await fetch ( '/api/upload' , { method: 'POST' , body: form }); } For server-rendered OG images that don't need a real browser, Vercel's @vercel/og is a different tool — see the FAQ below. Common gotchas "window is not defined" / "document is not defined" errors Import SnapDOM inside a browser event handler, as shown above, or load the capture component with dynamic(() => import('./CaptureCard'), { ssr: false }) from a client component. A 'use client' directive alone does not prevent prerendering. The captured image is blank in production but works in dev Check that the target is mounted, has a nonzero size and contains the expected data. Wait for layout-changing assets such as fonts. SnapDOM embeds used web fonts with embedFonts: 'auto' by default; a blank capture can have causes beyond font loading. Should I use SnapDOM or @vercel/og for OG images? Different tools. @vercel/og renders Satori-compatible JSX on the server (no real browser, no full CSS). SnapDOM runs client-side in a real browser and captures the rendered DOM exactly as the browser lays it out. Use @vercel/og when the card is fully described in JSX and you don't need real browser fidelity. Use SnapDOM when you want to capture a piece of your live UI with its current browser layout. Can I run SnapDOM in a server action? No. Server actions run in Node.js without a real DOM. Use Puppeteer or Playwright if you need server-side screenshots, and SnapDOM client-side. Cross-origin images break the capture Pass a CORS proxy via { useProxy: 'https://your-proxy.example.com/' } . SnapDOM will fetch external images through the proxy and inline them as data URLs. Does it work with Turbopack? SnapDOM has an ES module entry and no native runtime dependencies. Keep its import and capture calls inside the browser boundary when using Turbopack or Webpack. Always trigger the capture from a user event (button click) or inside useEffect after mount, never directly inside the component body. 2. Wait for application data and fonts to settle before capture if they can change the layout. Cross-origin images don't render SnapDOM fetches external images and inlines them as data URLs. If your CDN doesn't send Access-Control-Allow-Origin , configure a proxy with { useProxy: 'https://your-proxy.example.com/' } . Does SnapDOM work with React 18 strict mode? Yes. SnapDOM doesn't subscribe to React lifecycle, so the double-invocation in development strict mode doesn't affect captures triggered from event handlers. Can I use SnapDOM in Next.js? Yes — use a client component ( 'use client' ) and a dynamic import. See the dedicated Next.js guide . Does SnapDOM work with React Native? No. SnapDOM is a browser-only library — it relies on DOM APIs and SVG foreignObject that don't exist in React Native. How to read it One output stage for everyone. Every library is timed through to a PNG data URL, so no side skips rasterization and encoding. Cold and repeat are different numbers. First capture builds a new element per run; Repeat captures the same one again. Reuse can change timing and ranking, so read both columns. Defaults, scale 1. SnapDOM loads from @latest ; competitors use fixed versions. No library is configured for advantage. SnapDOM's automatic repeat memoization is off in every scene except Polling , so a cached result never races everyone else's full pipeline. The table does not know who should win. Rows sort by measured time and the fastest is highlighted, whoever it is. On some scenes that is not SnapDOM. Absolute milliseconds depend on your CPU, browser and how busy the machine is. Quote the ratios. Scene Run benchmark Copy results as markdown The page is held still during a run: a library that clones the whole document crops at viewport-relative coordinates, and scrolling mid-capture would move the region. Library First capture Repeat vs fastest Output Differs from SnapDOM The last column is the share of pixels that differ from SnapDOM's capture beyond a per-channel tolerance. It is not a correctness verdict: SnapDOM is the reference only because this page ships it. Small differences may be antialiasing, font rasterization or a real defect. A large number means the two did not render the same thing; the gallery below shows which. Milliseconds cannot tell a fast capture from a fast capture of the wrong thing . Every row must also produce the same output size and paint something. Not comparable means a different resolution; blank output means a correctly sized image with nothing in it. Either way the milliseconds measure the wrong thing. Treat those rows as bug reports, not results. What each library produced. Click one to open it full size. Speed is half the comparison; this is the other half. Capability matrix, verified by pixels Feature tables are usually copied from READMEs. This one captures a fixture where each capability paints its own marker colour, then counts those pixels in the output. "Supported" here means the colour survived the round trip. It starts by proving the oracle can say no : the same fixture is built with every capability removed, and all six must read absent. A checker that cannot fail means nothing. Run the capability matrix The oracle self-test runs first. Cells report behaviour with defaults . Some libraries pass more once configured; html2canvas handles conic gradients with foreignObjectRendering: true . Results vary by engine too: try Safari and Firefox. What this page cannot tell you It is one machine: yours. A busy laptop, a background tab or an extension injecting stylesheets will move every row. Run it twice. Competitors load from a CDN. Anything jsDelivr cannot serve shows up as a row that could not load, not as a win. Speed is not fidelity. A library that skips shadow DOM has less work to do. Read the output gallery and the capability matrix alongside the milliseconds. These are synthetic scenes. Each isolates a cost (per-node work, author-stylesheet scanning, shadow traversal, large-output raster). None of them is your page. The same scenes run in the repository as __tests__/category.*.benchmark.js .
